title: The constant-acceleration model
learning_outcomes: State the conditions under which constant-acceleration equations model motion.
Identify initial velocity, final velocity, acceleration, displacement and time with signs and units.
Derive v = u + at from the definition of acceleration.
Derive s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2 and v^2 = u^2 + 2as for straight-line motion with constant acceleration.
Explain why a term disappears when an initial condition is zero.
prior_knowledge_summary: From 9702_t02_cm02_l05, students can use signed area under a velocity-time graph to find displacement and can distinguish displacement from distance.
From 9702_t02_cm02_l04, students know that velocity-time gradient gives acceleration.
From 9702_t02_cm01_l02, students know 9702_def_acceleration and the meanings and units of velocity and acceleration.
new_learning: The equations in this lesson require straight-line motion with constant acceleration.
u and v describe the velocities at the start and end of the chosen time interval.
A zero initial condition removes its term from an equation.
not_yet_taught: A systematic routine for choosing and rearranging an equation in unfamiliar calculations
Free fall and vertical sign conventions
knowledge_boundary: This lesson builds and interprets the constant-acceleration equations for one straight-line interval. It uses small substitutions only to expose meaning. It does not teach the full equation-selection routine, linked stages, free fall or projectile motion.

mapped_demands: State that acceleration must be constant for a supplied equation to apply.
Recognise that a missing initial-velocity term means the object starts from rest.
Interpret a rearranged constant-acceleration equation without treating it as universally valid.
evidence_basis.syllabus_gap: The mapped P2 evidence tests conditions and interpretation but does not directly test derivation, so the derivations are supplied explicitly from the controlled definitions and graph knowledge.
evidence_basis.originality_note: Contexts, values and explanations are original. Evidence informs assessment demand only.
evidence_basis.canonical_audit: Checked both canonical condition-statement questions and mark schemes. Both directly support model validity and zero-initial-velocity interpretation.

requirements: Use simple marker lines, readable symbols and minimal labels.
Distribute visuals across the hook, model conditions, derivations, misconception and synthesis.
Vary sequence, graph, annotated area, comparison and equation-map forms.
Do not reveal practice answers or generate image assets.

blocks.title: Can one short rule predict the trolley?
body: A trolley enters a straight test track at 2.0 m s^-1. Its motor adds exactly 1.0 m s^-1 to the velocity every second.
Prediction: after 4.0 s, can we know its final velocity and displacement without drawing the whole journey second by second?
A compact model can do this, but only if the motion obeys strict conditions.

figure.purpose: Create the need for a compact model of steadily changing motion.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn four-frame trolley sequence on one straight track at equal one-second intervals. Velocity arrows lengthen evenly. Label only initial velocity and equal time steps.
figure.alt_text: A trolley moves along a straight track with a velocity arrow that grows by the same amount each second.

blocks.title: First decide whether the model fits
body: The motion must be along one straight line, so one signed direction is enough.
Acceleration must stay constant throughout the chosen time interval.
The interval needs clear initial conditions. Here u is the velocity at its start, not necessarily the velocity when the whole journey began.
If acceleration changes, these equations cannot describe the whole interval with one value of a. Split the motion only after multi-stage methods are taught.

figure.purpose: Contrast motion that fits the model with motion that does not.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn comparison table with a straight track and evenly growing velocity arrows under fits, a curving path and uneven arrow changes under does not fit. Add constant acceleration and one straight line labels only.
figure.alt_text: A comparison shows straight-line constant-acceleration motion beside curved or unevenly accelerated motion.

blocks.title: Name the five quantities
body: Choose a positive direction before assigning signs.
Initial and final refer to the start and end of the interval being modelled.
Displacement and velocity carry direction through their signs.

blocks.title: Build the velocity equation
body: Acceleration is rate of change of velocity.
For constant acceleration, a = (v - u) / t.
Multiply by t: at = v - u. Add u: v = u + at.
The term at is the velocity change during the interval. The equation says final velocity equals initial velocity plus velocity change.

figure.purpose: Connect constant velocity-time gradient to the first equation.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn straight velocity-time graph rising from u at time zero to v at time t. Mark vertical change v minus u, horizontal change t and gradient a. Place the three algebra steps beside it.
figure.alt_text: A straight velocity-time graph links its constant gradient to v equals u plus at.

blocks.title: Return to the trolley's velocity
body: For the trolley, u = +2.0 m s^-1, a = +1.0 m s^-2 and t = 4.0 s.
Use v = u + at.
The result matches the story: four equal one-second velocity increases add 4.0 m s^-1.

blocks.title: Build the displacement equation from area
body: Lesson 5 showed that signed area under a velocity-time graph gives displacement.
For constant acceleration, the graph is a straight line. Its area can be split into a rectangle and a triangle.
Rectangle area = ut. Triangle height is the velocity change at, so triangle area = 1/2 times t times at = 1/2 at^2.
Add the two signed areas: s = ut + 1/2 at^2.

figure.purpose: Make the two displacement terms visible as graph areas.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn velocity-time graph from u to v over time t. Split the area into a lightly hatched rectangle labelled ut and triangle labelled one half times t times at. Keep the axis and sign direction clear.
figure.alt_text: The area under a straight velocity-time line is split into rectangle ut and triangle one half at squared.

blocks.title: See the same displacement through average velocity
body: With constant acceleration, velocity changes evenly from u to v.
The average velocity is halfway between them: (u + v) / 2.
Displacement is average velocity times time, so s = (u + v)t / 2.
Substitute v = u + at. Then s = [u + (u + at)]t / 2 = ut + 1/2 at^2.
The graph-area route and the average-velocity route reach the same model.

figure.purpose: Give a second derivation of displacement using an evenly changing velocity sequence.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn number-line style velocity sequence from u to v with its midpoint labelled average velocity. Beside it, show displacement equals average velocity times time and the short substitution chain.
figure.alt_text: An evenly changing velocity sequence shows that average velocity is halfway between u and v.

blocks.title: Remove time when it is not part of the story
body: Start with s = (u + v)t / 2.
From v = u + at, the time is t = (v - u) / a when a is non-zero.
Substitute: s = (u + v)(v - u) / (2a).
Since (u + v)(v - u) = v^2 - u^2, 2as = v^2 - u^2.
Rearrange to v^2 = u^2 + 2as. This equation connects velocities and displacement without time.

blocks.title: A missing term is a clue, not magic
body: It can feel as if s = 1/2 at^2 is a separate formula that works whenever acceleration appears.
It is actually s = ut + 1/2 at^2 with u = 0. The object must start the chosen interval from rest, so ut becomes zero.
Likewise, v^2 = 2as comes from v^2 = u^2 + 2as when u = 0.
Constant acceleration and straight-line motion are still required. A missing term records a condition.

figure.purpose: Show how initial conditions simplify equations without changing their validity conditions.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn equation family tree. Start with the two full registered equations, branch through u equals zero, and end at their shortened forms. Put constant acceleration and straight line in a shared condition box.
figure.alt_text: An equation family tree shows that setting initial velocity to zero removes the initial-velocity terms.

blocks.title: One model, three views
items: v = u + at tracks how velocity changes with time.
s = ut + 1/2 at^2 tracks displacement with time.
v^2 = u^2 + 2as links velocity and displacement without time.
All three describe one straight-line interval with constant acceleration.
Read missing terms as information about initial conditions.

blocks.title: Resolve the trolley puzzle
body: The trolley's final velocity is +6.0 m s^-1.
We did not follow every second separately. Constant acceleration made the velocity-time graph straight, and that structure produced the equations.
The new mental model is conditional: compact equations are powerful because the motion is constrained, not because the equations work for every journey.

concepts_taught: Constant-acceleration equations model one straight-line interval with constant acceleration.
Initial and final values belong to the chosen interval.
The equations can be derived from acceleration and signed velocity-time area.
A zero initial condition removes its associated term.
misconceptions_addressed: Constant-acceleration equations work for changing acceleration.
Initial velocity always means the start of the entire journey.
A shortened equation is universally valid.
A missing term can be ignored without identifying the condition that makes it zero.
skills_students_can_now_use: State the validity conditions for constant-acceleration equations.
Identify u, v, a, s and t with signs and units.
Explain the derivation and meaning of the three registered equations.
Infer an initial condition from a missing term.
next_lesson_can_assume: Students know the three registered constant-acceleration equations and their symbols.
Students know that the equations require straight-line motion with constant acceleration.
Students can interpret zero initial velocity and explain why an initial-velocity term disappears.
Students understand that signs depend on the chosen positive direction.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: Students can independently choose the best equation from a list of knowns.
Students can confidently rearrange every equation in unfamiliar calculations.
Students can solve linked multi-stage or reverse problems.
Students know free-fall or projectile-motion conventions.
